kurz: How often annual forecasts are right, why they still appear every December and what can take the place of the point forecast.

bloecke.md:
Every year in December, forecasts of where the DAX and the S&P 500 will stand twelve months later appear in the same format. Banks supply a figure, editorial teams collect the figures, the financial dailies Handelsblatt and Börsen-Zeitung compile them in a table, and in January the outlook serves as a conversation opener in every advisory meeting. That the figures are wrong is to be expected. But they are often very far off, and the following December nobody comes back to them.

The hit rate can be checked. In the eight years from 2018 to 2025, the consensus estimate of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was at most ten percentage points away from the outcome in only a single year; in the other seven years it deviated by more. The largest single error came in 2022. A gain of 3.9% was expected, but the index lost 19.4%. The forecast was thus 23.3 percentage points off, and in the direction of a loss.

bloecke.titel: Consensus forecast and outcome for the S&P 500 (price performance excluding dividends)
Expected and actual performance of the S&P 500
bloecke.unter: In both years shown, the consensus was far off on the size of the change, and in one of the two years it also had the wrong sign.

bloecke.md: In most of the past 16 years, the consensus was too low, by around ten percentage points on average. When a forecast mostly misses in the same direction for a decade and a half, the error is systematic and not random. There are professional reasons for this. Strategists who stay close to the average of their peers can do little wrong. If, on the other hand, someone predicts a fall of 20% and is wrong, they lose mandates.

## Dispersion of annual results

A point forecast rests on two assumptions. First, the possible annual results cluster tightly around one value; second, this value can be hit. Even the first assumption is wrong, as can be checked with German data.

Between 1988 and 2025, the DAX performance index returned an arithmetic mean of 11.2% a year. In exactly eight of these 38 years, the result was within five percentage points of this mean. In 19 years, that is half of them, the index rose or fell by more than 20%. The mean therefore does not describe a typical year. It is the centre of gravity of a very wide distribution, and a forecast that names it predicts an outcome that almost never occurs in the market.

bloecke.unter: Only a few years lie close to the mean of 11.2%, while many deviate far upwards or downwards, so a single figure is poorly suited as a forecast.

bloecke.md: The mean is the result of a calculation, not an observed year. An annual forecast assumes that this time the result will lie near the middle of the distribution, although that rarely happens.

## Price targets and earnings estimates

For individual shares, the forecast is called a price target. At least it is based on a valuation model, but that does not make it any more reliable. Two patterns have been stable for decades. First, the aggregated earnings estimates for the current year start out too high and are lowered quarter by quarter. In the end, the company narrowly beats the lowered estimate, and the result is the headline “above expectations”. The surprise then relates to a figure that was deliberately lowered beforehand to an achievable level. Second, the ratings are unevenly distributed. Sell recommendations have traditionally made up only a low single-digit percentage of all analyst ratings, although usually more than half of all shares perform worse than the market weighted by market capitalisation.

The reason lies in conflicts of interest, which the legislator is also aware of. Investment recommendations are governed by Article 20 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) and specified in more detail in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/958. A recommendation must be presented objectively, its sources and valuation method must be identifiable, and its author must disclose conflicts of interest. These include, for example, the author's firm managing securities issues for the same company or holding a notifiable stake in it. In Germany, Section 85 WpHG (Securities Trading Act) supplements these obligations, and supervision lies with BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority). The disclosure is in small print at the end of the document. It does not remove the conflict, but it makes it visible to the reader.

bloecke.titel: The same finding for economic forecasts
bloecke.md: The joint economic forecast (Gemeinschaftsdiagnose) of the leading German economic research institutes, produced twice a year on behalf of the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, and the monthly ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment are methodologically far more careful than any bank forecast. At turning points in the economy, this is of little help. In autumn 2008, expectations for 2009 were far above what actually happened. German gross domestic product shrank by around 5.7% in real terms, the sharpest decline of the post-war period. The institutes cannot be blamed for this; at turning points, such a misjudgement is the norm. Forecasting models extrapolate existing relationships, and turning points are by definition the moments at which these relationships stop holding.

## Research on forecasters

The most robust study comes from outside the financial industry. Over around two decades, the psychologist Philip Tetlock collected just over 80,000 dated, verifiable forecasts from 284 experts in politics, economics and security, and analysed them in 2005 in *Expert Political Judgment*. On average, the experts were no better than simple statistical extrapolations, and the longer the forecasting horizon, the closer their results came to pure guessing.

Within the group, however, there were large differences. Using an image from Isaiah Berlin, Tetlock divided his experts into hedgehogs and foxes. The hedgehog knows one big thing, explains the world from a single principle and is in demand in the media because it makes clear statements. The fox knows many small things, thinks in probabilities and corrects itself as soon as new data are available. The foxes were consistently better calibrated. In addition, an expert's prominence was negatively related to their accuracy: the experts with the most media appearances made worse forecasts on average.

Tetlock's later research shows how forecasts can be improved. In a forecasting tournament run by the US research agency IARPA that began in 2011, his Good Judgment Project identified a small group of laypeople who consistently performed better than the other participants. According to published reports, these laypeople were also better than intelligence analysts with access to classified information. The “superforecasters” had no better information; they went about it differently. They broke a question down into sub-questions, started with the base rate instead of gut feeling, gave probabilities in fine gradations and frequently adjusted their assessments in small steps.

bloecke.erklaerung: The Brier score measures how well the stated probabilities match the outcomes that occurred, instead of merely counting hits. Smaller values are better; zero would be perfect.
variablen: stated probability of the event, between 0 and 1
outcome: 1 if it occurred, 0 if not
bloecke.beispiel: Anyone who says 50% for every question always ends up with 0.25. This is the benchmark for a forecast made without any knowledge. A stated 90% contributes 0.01 if the event occurs and 0.81 if it does not. The scale harshly punishes great confidence in wrong forecasts and rewards honestly stated uncertainty. (Tetlock uses a two-sided variant in which guessing yields 0.5 instead of 0.25. This does not change the ranking.)

bloecke.md:
In December, forecaster A says: “The DAX will stand at 26,000 at the end of next year.” Forecaster B says: “With a probability of 70%, the annual result will lie between minus 15% and plus 30%.” At the end of the year, the result is a gain of 6%.

A was obviously wrong, but A's error cannot be scored. Without a probability there is nothing to calculate with. This explains why point forecasts survive for so long. They can be refuted in an individual case, but they cannot be graded over a longer period. B gave the probability p = 0.7 to an event that occurred and adds (0.7 − 1)² = 0.09 to their Brier score. After twenty such years, B can be graded, but A cannot, even then.

## Reasons for the annual forecasts

The demand is genuine, because uncertainty is unpleasant and a figure feels like an answer. On the supply side, four mechanisms come into play as well.

- There is no accounting for errors. Hardly any forecast is publicly evaluated a year later. Poor calibration therefore has no consequences.
- The payoff is asymmetric. A bold forecast that comes true can make a career. If the same forecast fails, it is never mentioned again. As long as nobody keeps count, a bold forecast carries no risk.
- Forecasts serve sales. An annual outlook advertises the firm's business, that is, advice, securities accounts, funds or certificates. A market assessment is an occasion for a client meeting.
- Reallocations generate revenue. Every forecast that is followed triggers transactions, and the income from them accrues whether the forecast is right or not.

Stays unchanged, because consistency counts as competence.

bloecke.md:
## From point forecast to range

Thinking about the future is possible without a point forecast, but in a different form. For investment products, the European legislator has already made this step mandatory. The key information document (KID) under the PRIIPs Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014), fleshed out in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/653, prohibits the single figure and prescribes four scenarios (stress, unfavourable, moderate, favourable), each related to the recommended holding period. For marketing material, Article 44 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 also applies. Under it, information on future performance must be based on reasonable assumptions, must not be based on simulated past performance and needs a prominent warning that it is not a reliable indicator.

Even so, the scenarios should be read with caution. The methodology derives them from historical returns, so after long upward phases they turn out too favourable. For this reason, the methodology was revised, and the new version has applied since the beginning of 2023. The scenarios are above all a formal requirement, but they have a useful side effect, because they force a range to be shown instead of a single figure. Private investors can take the same approach for their own planning, for example with a [[Monte Carlo simulation]] that generates thousands of possible paths from the [[Return|return]] and [[Standard deviation|standard deviation]] instead of extrapolating a constant interest rate.

bloecke.titel: Predictability and effect on final wealth
bloecke.unter: Almost all topics of the annual outlooks lie in the bottom-left field, so they are hard to predict and almost irrelevant to final wealth.

felder.titel: Market return over the next ten years, timing of a crash, turn in the interest rate cycle
felder.text: Large effect, cannot be planned. Protection: diversification, buffers and an allocation you can withstand in a [[Maximum drawdown|maximum drawdown]].

felder.titel: Savings amount, expense ratio, investment period, tax burden, trading frequency
felder.text: Large effect, known in advance. Only here can you plan effectively.

felder.titel: DAX on 31 Dec, one share’s quarterly profit, ECB meeting
felder.text: Hardly predictable, of little relevance individually. Main topic of the annual outlooks.

felder.titel: Distribution dates, index changes, annual general meetings
felder.text: Reliably known and of minor importance.

bloecke.md:
1. The forecast should state a probability. Without one, the statement cannot be checked afterwards.
2. It also needs a date and a measurable criterion. Terms such as “in the medium term” and “significant correction” merely convey a mood.
3. Establish who produces the forecast and what this firm then sells. The disclosure under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/958 is usually on the last page.
4. The same firm's forecast from twelve months ago can be compared with the outcome. This comparison is almost always more revealing than the new figure.

mitnehmen: From 2018 to 2025, the consensus forecast of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was within ten percentage points of the outcome in only one of eight years, and in most of the last 16 years it was too low.
Point forecasts fail because of their format, even when the work is careful: of 38 DAX years, only eight were close to the mean, and half moved by more than 20%.

According to Tetlock's findings, experts on average do not beat a simple extrapolation, self-confidence is negatively related to accuracy, and forecasters who think in probabilities and revise their assessments are better calibrated.
Only a stated probability makes a forecast assessable with the Brier score, and a forecaster who does not state one evades assessment.

For investment products, the European legislator prescribes four scenarios instead of one figure in the key information document, and in private planning the equivalent is a range instead of a fixed interest rate.

begriffe.text: Forecast that states exactly one value for a point in time, such as an index level at the end of the year. Without a stated probability, it cannot be assessed afterwards.

Average of all recorded individual forecasts by analysts or strategists for a quantity such as an index level, earnings per share or an interest rate. It serves as a benchmark, and deviations from it are regarded as a surprise.
Measure of the quality of probability forecasts. It is the mean squared distance between the stated probability and the actual outcome. Zero is perfect; always guessing 50% gives 0.25.
A forecaster is well calibrated if, of all the events to which they gave 70%, around 70% actually occurred in the end. Calibration is independent of how boldly someone forecasts.

Historical frequency of an event without taking the current situation into account. It is the starting point of every well-calibrated forecast and is the thing most often overlooked in poor forecasts.
One of the four legally required performance presentations in the key information document under the PRIIPs Regulation. The four scenarios are called stress, unfavourable, moderate and favourable.
